questions.q: Identify the narrative tense predominantly used in the story and name the grammatical term for the tense used when the narrator recalls his mother's death ("Nearly six years ago, before leaving for London, I had watched her die...").
questions.a: The predominant narrative tense is the simple past (e.g., "I left," "I lived," "I attended"). The tense used for the mother's death is the past perfect ("had watched"), which indicates an event that occurred before the main narrative timeline. A wrong answer (e.g., saying "past continuous" or "present perfect") reveals confusion about narrative time management and the function of past perfect for anterior events in a past-tense narrative.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the narrator says "I was on a budget all the same" after stating he was "no longer a student." What does the phrase "all the same" signal grammatically and pragmatically?
questions.a: "All the same" is a discourse marker (conjunctive adverbial) meaning "nevertheless" or "despite that." It signals a concession: the narrator acknowledges he is not a student (so the student guidebook might not apply) but asserts the financial constraint remains. A wrong answer that treats "all the same" as a time phrase or ignores the contrast shows inability to recognize pragmatic markers that structure argumentation in narrative prose.

questions.q: In the dialogue with Mrs Croft, she says: "Fasten the chain and firmly press that button on the knob!" Identify the sentence type, the verb forms, and the pragmatic force. Then rewrite it as an indirect speech report suitable for a formal narrative summary.
questions.a: Sentence type: compound imperative (two coordinate clauses). Verb forms: base form "fasten" and "press" (imperative mood). Pragmatic force: direct command with authority. Indirect speech: "She ordered me to fasten the chain and to press the button on the knob firmly." A wrong answer that uses "told me fasten" (missing "to") or changes "firmly" to "firm" reveals gaps in imperative-to-infinitive transformation and adverb placement in reported speech.

questions.q: Compare the narrator's internal monologue (e.g., "I was too tired to pace...") with his spoken dialogue (e.g., "Yes, madame."). Analyze how syntax, vocabulary, and sentence length differ, and explain what this contrast reveals about his psychological state and social position.
questions.a: Internal monologue uses complex sentences, subordinate clauses ("As I stepped into the house..."), precise descriptive vocabulary ("stifling," "suffocating"), and first-person reflection. Spoken dialogue is elliptical, honorific-heavy ("madame"), and syntactically simple ("Yes, madame."). The contrast reveals the narrator's rich interiority versus his constrained, deferential public performance as a new immigrant. A wrong answer that only notes "one is long, one is short" misses the syntactic and sociolinguistic significance.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of Lahiri's use of British vs. American lexical pairs (lift/elevator, engaged/busy, torch/flashlight) in the guidebook passage. Does it merely convey information, or does it serve a deeper narrative function? Justify your judgment.
questions.a: It serves a deeper function: the list enacts the narrator's cognitive transition, positioning him (and the reader) between two linguistic worlds. The guidebook's authoritative tone ("Americans drove on the right... they called a lift an elevator") mirrors the institutional voice that governs immigrant life. A weak evaluation treats it as mere vocabulary listing; a strong one connects lexical contrast to the theme of displacement and the narrator's liminal identity.

questions.q: Write a short paragraph (5-6 sentences) continuing the story from the narrator's perspective, ten years later, maintaining the same grammatical voice: past tense narration, occasional past perfect for earlier memories, formal register with Indian English honorifics ("madame," "sir"), and at least one British/American lexical contrast.
questions.a: A successful paragraph will use consistent past tense narration ("I walked," "I remembered"), deploy past perfect for a memory prior to that moment ("I had not visited Mrs Croft's street since..."), include an honorific in recalled or imagined dialogue ("Good morning, sir"), and embed a lexical contrast ("I took the lift—elevator, I corrected myself—to the tenth floor"). A poor answer will slip into present tense, omit honorifics, or lack the lexical contrast, showing failure to internalize the narrator's linguistic fingerprint.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Language Usage in the Text refers to the systematic analysis of grammatical structures, lexical choices, and syntactic patterns that an author employs to construct narrative voice, ______ individuals, establish cultural settings, and convey thematic concerns.
Fill in the blank: ______ you are listening to a friend who has just moved from a small town in India to a bustling city abroad.
What is Language Usage in the Text? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Language Usage in the Text refers to the systematic analysis of grammatical structures, lexical choices, and syntactic patterns that an author employs to construct narrative voice, characterize individuals, establish cultural settings, and convey thematic concerns.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Language Usage in the Text?
questions.a: Students often think "language usage" means only identifying parts of speech (nouns, verbs) or listing British/American word pairs.
